decisions.reason: Not relevant to the brief: this is a conference-prep post about MAICON logistics and personal health tips, not evidence about AI tools for customer, competitor, or market research. Credibility is limited for our use because it is a self-promotional piece from the conference organizer/related commentator, with no methods, data, or inspectable evidence supporting any research-tool claim. No material uncertainty beyond irrelevance.

Relevant only as generic AI safety news, not to the central question of which AI tools help small businesses do customer/competitor/market research reliably and cheaply. The piece is a reported incident story from TechCrunch, but it offers no workflow, baseline, cost, or methods for evaluating research usefulness; the underlying claim is also about law-enforcement misuse, not research capability. It is a single vendor-incident report with no performance evidence, so uncertainty remains high and it does not advance the brief.

Primarily speculative opinion rather than inspectable evidence: it extrapolates from cognitive-offloading and military-AI anecdotes into end-of-world scenarios. For our brief, the piece is not about small-business research workflows, and its cited claims are not independently demonstrated here; several references are just name-dropped receipts rather than verified comparative evidence. The author also has clear commercial incentives (course, Slack group, consulting brand promotion), which further limits usefulness for editorial acceptance.

This is a promotional conference-guide article for MAICON, not substantive evidence about AI research tools or methods. It is highly commercial, aimed at attendance and sponsor engagement, and contains logistics, networking, and sponsor-callout content rather than inspectable research workflows, accuracy data, or cost comparisons. No methods or uncertain claims relevant to the brief are presented.
